title: USD 250,000, no account relationship, and the wrong route chosen
explain:
A Canadian bank had to pay USD 250,000 to a United States beneficiary.
It held its dollars with Wells Fargo.
The beneficiary held its account with Citibank New York.
The bank sent a single serial MT103, and the payment had nowhere to settle.

Here's how that happens:

→ Canadian bank holds USD with Wells Fargo
→ Beneficiary holds account with Citibank
→ No account relationship between the sending bank and Citibank
→ Serial MT103 sent, settlement fails

The assumption was:
"One MT103 reaches any beneficiary."
Account relationships decide serial or cover.

Why?

Because the sending bank had no account relationship with Citibank, the correct route was a cover payment: an MT103 sent directly to Citibank and an MT202 COV sent to Wells Fargo. If the sending bank had held an account with the beneficiary's bank, a single serial MT103 would have been enough.

Account relationships decide the route. No relationship means cover, not serial.

What proves the chosen route matches the account relationships?

BA Takeaway

Check the account relationships before choosing the route. No direct relationship with the beneficiary's bank means cover: MT103 to the beneficiary bank, MT202 COV to the bank holding the funds.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Sending bank accounts
→ Beneficiary bank accounts
→ Direct relationship or not
→ Route chosen

The real requirement isn't "Can we send one MT103?"

It's "What evidence proves the chosen route matches the account relationships?"

Have you ever seen a payment fail because the route ignored the account relationships?
takeaway: Account relationships decide the route. No relationship means cover, not serial.

title: EUR 100,000 MT103 refused before it was even read
explain:
EUR 100,000 was due to a beneficiary.
The MT103 was sent.
The receiving bank's system refused it outright, before anyone read it, because no RMA existed for the sender.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 sent to the beneficiary bank
→ No RMA set up for the sender
→ Receiving system refuses the message
→ Payment never starts

The assumption was:
"The RMA can be sorted out afterwards."
Without an RMA the receiving bank's system will not accept the message.

Why?

Before one bank can send an MT103 to another over SWIFT, the receiving bank must set up an RMA, a relationship management authorisation, for that sender. The RMA is therefore a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

The RMA is a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

What proves the RMA is in place before the MT103 is sent?

BA Takeaway

Ask the beneficiary bank to establish the RMA before the payment is sent. Check it before sending, and never promise a payment date until the authorisation exists.

Keep these controls separate:

→ RMA in place
→ MT103 sent
→ Message accepted
→ Payment on its way

The real requirement isn't "Can we send the MT103 now?"

It's "What evidence proves the RMA is in place before the MT103 is sent?"

Have you ever had a payment refused because the RMA was missing?
takeaway: The RMA is a precondition for the payment, not a formality that can be sorted out afterwards.

title: USD 175,000 took the long route when a shorter one was on file
explain:
USD 175,000 was sent by the preferred route.
It took three days.
A shorter route was on file the whole time, and no one used it because the preferred instruction felt like an order.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank publishes several SSIs for USD
→ One route marked as preferred
→ Sender uses the preferred route by default
→ Beneficiary waits three days, shorter route unused

The assumption was:
"Preferred means we must use it."
The preferred route is an option, not an order.

Why?

A bank can publish several standing settlement instructions for one currency, marking one as preferred, but the preferred route is an option, not an order. The sender may use a shorter route, even one that passes through a bank named in a non-preferred instruction, because the aim is for the funds to reach the beneficiary.

Preferred is an option, not an order. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one will complain.

What proves we chose the route that pays the beneficiary fastest?

BA Takeaway

Compare the routes on file before sending. Use the shorter route when it pays the beneficiary faster, even if it runs through a bank named in a non-preferred instruction.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Routes on file
→ Preferred route
→ Shorter route
→ Beneficiary paid fastest

The real requirement isn't "Which route should we use?"

It's "What evidence proves we chose the route that pays the beneficiary fastest?"

Have you ever watched a payment take the long route when a shorter one was on file?
takeaway: Preferred is an option, not an order. If the beneficiary is paid faster on the shorter route, no one will complain.

title: EUR 95,000 drawn on the parent's account with no authority on file
explain:
A subsidiary instructed a EUR 95,000 payment from its parent company's account.
The payment went through.
No authorisation was on file, and the parent only found out when the statement arrived.

Here's how that happens:

→ Subsidiary wants to use the parent's account
→ No authorisation on file
→ Payment drawn from the parent's account
→ Parent learns of it from the statement

The assumption was:
"A subsidiary can use the parent's account. It is the same group."
An authorisation is required before the subsidiary may draw on the parent's account.

Why?

In the MT101 the subsidiary appears as the Instructing Party in field 50L, while the parent company appears as the ordering customer in field 50H, because the parent owns the account that will be debited. The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender of an instruction is not the owner of the account being debited.

The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender is not the owner of the account being debited.

What proves the sender was authorised to draw on this account?

BA Takeaway

Check the authorisation before debiting an account for a sender who does not own it. Record the subsidiary as Instructing Party in field 50L and the parent as ordering customer in field 50H, and never debit on group membership alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Authorisation on file
→ Instructing Party in field 50L
→ Ordering customer in field 50H
→ Account owner confirmed

The real requirement isn't "Can the subsidiary use this account?"

It's "What evidence proves the sender was authorised to draw on this account?"

Have you ever found a payment drawn on an account with no authority on file?
takeaway: The same need for authorisation applies whenever the sender is not the owner of the account being debited.

title: An FX deal for EUR 800,000 settled a day late. The trade was placed at 4pm.
explain:
A EUR 800,000 FX deal is traded late in the day.
The team expects settlement on the tenor date.
The funds arrive a day later, and a payment misses its value date.

Here is how that happens:

→ FX deal traded after the cut-off
→ Tenor counted from the trade day
→ Settlement slips by one day
→ Payment misses its value date

The requirement said:
"An FX tenor always counts from the trade day."

Why?

An FX tenor such as Today, Tomorrow or Spot counts from the day the deal is traded, provided the trade happens before the FX cut-off time. Traded today before the cut-off, a Today tenor settles today, a Tomorrow tenor settles tomorrow, and Spot settles in two days or more. A trade after the cut-off settles a day later, because once the cut-off passes the bank is already working on the next day.

After the cut-off, the trade day is tomorrow.

BA Takeaway

Check the cut-off before promising any FX settlement date, and say so plainly when a trade lands after it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Trade time
→ FX cut-off
→ Tenor settlement date

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this trade was placed before the cut-off?"

Have you promised a settlement date that the cut-off had already moved?
takeaway: After the cut-off, the trade day is tomorrow.

title: Collections moved to D-1 to be faster. EUR 90,000 of collections failed on day one.
explain:
A creditor moves direct debit submission forward to D-1.
EUR 90,000 of collections go out on the new date.
They fail at the first step, because the file cut-off and the scheme calendar were never checked.

Here is how that happens:

→ Submission moved forward to D-1
→ EUR 90,000 of collections submitted
→ Scheme calendar and file cut-off never validated
→ Collections fail at the first step

The requirement said:
"Moving a date forward is a diary change."

Why?

Bringing direct debit submission forward to D-1 is an operational commitment, not a diary change. Four things must support the earlier date, the scheme calendar, the file cut-off, the bank processing window and operational capacity, or collections fail at the first step. Verify all four before moving the date, because a date the infrastructure cannot meet turns into rejects, complaints and refunds.

D-1 is an operational commitment, not a diary change.

BA Takeaway

Prove all four readiness checks before any submission date moves, and name the owner of each check.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme calendar
→ File cut-off
→ Bank processing window
→ Operational capacity

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the infrastructure can meet this earlier date?"

Have you moved a submission date that the systems could not meet?
takeaway: D-1 is an operational commitment, not a diary change.

title: A Request to Pay for EUR 3,000 had no date. Three systems settled it on three different days.
explain:
A SEPA Request to Pay for EUR 3,000 arrives with no requested execution date.
One system derives a date, one asks the customer, one applies a rule.
The same request settles on three different dates.

Here is how that happens:

→ Request to Pay for EUR 3,000 received
→ No requested execution date on the request
→ Each system derives its own date
→ Same request settles on different dates

The requirement said:
"The payment date can be left to each system to work out."

Why?

Without a requested execution date a SEPA Request to Pay has no payment date, so one must be derived, chosen by the customer, or validated against a rule. Unless derivation, choice and validation are all defined, the same request settles on different dates in different systems. Execution then follows the agreed date, and a date that fails validation is rejected before it ever reaches the scheme.

No date on the request means no single payment date.

BA Takeaway

Define derivation, customer choice and validation for the execution date before the first Request to Pay is accepted.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Date derivation rule
→ Customer date choice
→ Date validation

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves which date this request must settle on?"

Have you seen one request settle on different dates in different systems?
takeaway: No date on the request means no single payment date.

title: A EUR 500,000 payment passed sanctions. The check that should have run first ran last.
explain:
A EUR 500,000 payment is screened by four controls.
The controls were reordered for speed, and one ran after the payment it was meant to stop.
The payment passes, and the control that assumed a predecessor had run never fires.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 500,000 payment enters screening
→ Controls reordered from sequential to parallel
→ One control assumes a predecessor has run
→ Bad payment passes the gap

The requirement said:
"Control order is a performance tweak."

Why?

Running payment controls sequentially or in parallel is a risk decision, not a performance tweak: it changes latency, risk coverage and behaviour under load. Sequential controls are slower but easy to reason about, since each waits for its predecessor, while parallel controls are faster but demand explicit rules for one control failing while another passes. Map control dependencies first, because a control that assumes a predecessor has run will pass bad payments the moment the order changes.

Control order is a risk decision, not a performance tweak.

BA Takeaway

Map control dependencies before any control is reordered, and write the rule for a control that fails while another passes.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Control dependencies
→ Sequential order
→ Parallel failure rules

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves no control runs ahead of the control it depends on?"

Have you reordered controls and opened a gap a bad payment walked through?
takeaway: Control order is a risk decision, not a performance tweak.

title: EUR 70,000 held on a party name that looked wrong. The team rejected it outright.
explain:
A EUR 70,000 payment arrives with ultimate debtor details that look wrong, but are not proven wrong.
The team rejects it outright.
A legitimate payment dies, and the customer loses a supplier deadline.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 70,000 payment with uncertain party details
→ Details look wrong but are not proven wrong
→ Payment rejected outright
→ Legitimate payment lost

The requirement said:
"Uncertain details mean reject the payment."

Why?

Ultimate debtor or creditor details that look wrong but are not proven wrong call for a question, not a rejection, because rejecting outright can kill a legitimate payment. Park the payment under a clear status, request the additional information back up the chain, and give the sender a bounded window to answer. Clean facts release it, confirmed problems mean rejection or return depending on settlement state, and a missed deadline falls back to the policy default.

Uncertain means ask, not kill.

BA Takeaway

Park uncertain payments with a clear status, ask up the chain, and decide only on the facts that come back.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Party details under question
→ Information request
→ Bounded answer window

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves these details are wrong, not just uncertain?"

Have you killed a legitimate payment by rejecting what you should have questioned?
takeaway: Uncertain means ask, not kill.

title: EUR 180,000 was covered but never credited. The instruction and the money took different roads.
explain:
A EUR 180,000 cross-border payment is sent by cover.
The pacs.009 cover arrives, but the pacs.008 instruction does not.
The beneficiary bank cannot credit the customer, and the money sits unmatched.

Here is how that happens:

→ pacs.008 instruction sent
→ pacs.009 COVE cover sent separately
→ Cover arrives, instruction does not
→ Beneficiary bank cannot credit the customer

The requirement said:
"If the cover arrives, the customer can be credited."

Why?

The cover method splits the payment in two: the pacs.008 carries customer details to the beneficiary bank, while the pacs.009 with settlement method COVE moves the funds through correspondents, the pair linked by one UETR. A sanctions hold on either leg stops the whole payment, because the beneficiary bank may credit the customer only when both legs reconcile. A cover that arrives alone parks as an unmatched item until its instruction completes the pair.

Instruction one way, money another. Both must arrive.

BA Takeaway

Reconcile the pacs.008 and the pacs.009 as a pair on one UETR, and never credit on the cover alone.

Keep these controls separate:

→ pacs.008 instruction
→ pacs.009 cover
→ UETR pair

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves both legs of this cover payment have arrived and reconciled?"

Have you seen a cover arrive alone and sit unmatched?
takeaway: Instruction one way, money another. Both must arrive.

title: A EUR 300,000 payment went quiet for a day. Nobody owned it, and nobody called the customer.
explain:
A EUR 300,000 payment passes its expected window with no status update.
It sits on a dashboard, flagged but unowned.
The deadline passes, the customer calls first, and the team starts from zero.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 300,000 payment passes its expected window
→ No status update from the tracker
→ Flag raised with no owner
→ Customer calls before the team acts

The requirement said:
"A dashboard flag is enough to manage at-risk payments."

Why?

At-risk has a precise meaning: no status update within the expected window for that corridor and amount, drawn from the tracker, pacs.002 statuses and internal hop timestamps. Every flagged payment needs a named owner, operations, the relationship manager, or investigations, and action before the deadline, reroute, chase the intermediary, or warn the customer early. A dashboard of unowned flags is decoration; a flag works only with an owner and a next action.

A flag without an owner is decoration.

BA Takeaway

Give every at-risk flag a named owner and a next action before the deadline, and warn the customer early.

Keep these controls separate:

→ At-risk definition
→ Named owner
→ Next action

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payment is owned and being worked?"

Have you watched a flagged payment sit unowned until the customer called?
takeaway: A flag without an owner is decoration.

title: A surname parked a 28 million dirham letter of credit for 8 working days.
explain:
A legitimate 28 million dirham letter of credit is stopped by a fuzzy sanctions match on a common surname.
It sits parked for 8 working days.
The screening team treats every alert the same, and the real business waits.

Here is how that happens:

→ 28 million dirham letter of credit presented
→ Fuzzy match on a common surname
→ Payment parked for 8 working days
→ Every alert treated the same

The requirement said:
"Every sanctions alert deserves the same attention."

Why?

Sanctions screening is a false-positive business: about 95 percent of alerts are false positives, yet each one delays real business, and a fuzzy match on a common surname parked a legitimate 28 million dirham letter of credit for 8 working days. The answer is risk triage, exact matches and high-risk corridors first, with matching thresholds tuned per corridor and name frequency instead of one global setting. Judge the screening flow on its KPIs, the false-positive rate and the average hold time, and measure and report both.

Most alerts are false positives. Triage by risk, not by queue order.

BA Takeaway

Triage screening alerts by risk, tune thresholds per corridor, and report the false-positive rate and the hold time.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Alert triage
→ Matching thresholds
→ Hold time KPI

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this alert was triaged by risk, not just queued?"

Have you seen a real deal parked for days on a common surname?
takeaway: Most alerts are false positives. Triage by risk, not by queue order.

title: A USD 500,000 payment matched the sanctions list. The funds froze, and the trail mattered.
explain:
A USD 500,000 payment matches a name on the sanctions list.
The payment is held at once and no funds move.
The analyst wonders whether to release it quietly and move on.

Here is how that happens:

→ USD 500,000 payment screened
→ Name matches the sanctions list
→ Payment held immediately
→ Analyst considers releasing it without a trail

The requirement said:
"A sanctions hold is a pause, not a case."

Why?

A sanctions list match stops the payment at once: it is held immediately and no funds move while the review is open. The analyst escalates to the compliance officer with the match evidence attached, and true-match verification decides the path, release if false, block if true. Where the activity meets the threshold a Suspicious Activity Report is filed, and every step is documented, because the decision trail is what regulators will ask for.

A list match stops the payment. The trail proves the decision.

BA Takeaway

Hold on a match, escalate with the evidence, verify the true match, and document every step.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Match evidence
→ True match verification
→ Decision trail

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this match was verified, not just held or released?"

Have you held a payment on a list match with no documented trail?
takeaway: A list match stops the payment. The trail proves the decision.

title: USD 85,000 left a customer's account. The bank called it authorised, and refused to pay it back.
explain:
A scammer posing as a bank representative wins remote access to a victim's computer.
USD 85,000 leaves from the victim's own login and device.
The bank classifies the payment as authorised, and the customer loses everything.

Here is how that happens:

→ Scammer poses as a bank representative
→ Remote access won to the victim computer
→ USD 85,000 sent from the victim's own login
→ Bank refuses reimbursement as authorised

The requirement said:
"A payment sent by the victim must be refunded."

Why?

Authorised push payment fraud exploits the gap between a valid payment and a deceived customer. A scammer posing as a bank representative won remote access to the victim computer, and the wire left from the victim's own login and device, so the bank classified it as authorised and refused reimbursement. The defences are confirmation of payee, friction on first-time payees, warnings at the point of payment, and behavioural detection, and the regulatory trend is shifting liability back toward banks.

Valid payment, deceived customer. Authorised is not the same as safe.

BA Takeaway

Build the defences before the payment, not the argument after it: confirmation of payee, friction on first-time payees, warnings and behavioural detection.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Confirmation of payee
→ First-time payee friction
→ Point of payment warnings

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this payee was checked before the money left?"

Have you seen a customer lose money on a payment the system called valid?
takeaway: Valid payment, deceived customer. Authorised is not the same as safe.

title: One mule account looked like a case. Linked together, they were a network moving millions.
explain:
Small transfers arrive from unrelated sources into one account.
The funds leave within minutes of credit, and almost nothing is retained.
The team treats the account as a single case, while the network keeps moving.

Here is how that happens:

→ Small inward transfers from unrelated sources
→ Funds moved out within minutes of credit
→ Minimal balance retention
→ Common device and IP linkage across accounts

The requirement said:
"One suspicious account is one case to close."

Why?

A mule network is a pattern, not an account: small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device or IP linkage. One account is a case, linked accounts are a network, so freeze suspect accounts on debit first, then run EDD and KYC reviews and escalate to investigations. Recalibrate detection rules so the pattern is caught earlier next time, without punishing genuine customers.

Read the network, not the case.

BA Takeaway

Freeze on debit first, then link the accounts, run EDD and KYC, and recalibrate the rules to catch the pattern earlier.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Network linkage
→ Debit freeze
→ EDD and KYC review

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves these accounts are linked, not just individually suspicious?"

Have you closed one mule account while the network kept moving?
takeaway: Read the network, not the case.

title: Due date 15 October. Five calendars broke, and the SDD timeline broke with them.
explain:
A collection is due on 15 October, with due date, settlement date and debit date all the same.
A new national holiday is declared after planning, and one PSP is closed.
The team assumes the due date moves, and the collection fails.

Here is how that happens:

→ Collection due 15 October
→ Creditor PSP closed, TARGET open
→ New national holiday declared after planning
→ Team assumes the due date moves

The requirement said:
"On a normal due date, the timeline takes care of itself."

Why?

On a normal due date the due date, settlement date and debit date are the same, but the timeline breaks when calendars do not align. Five scenarios test it for a single due date: the creditor PSP closed, TARGET or the CSM closed, the debtor PSP closed, both PSPs closed, and a new national holiday declared after planning. In each case the BA must ask which parties are open, what activity needs to happen and which calendar applies, rather than assuming which date moves, because a good SDD timeline is designed for the broken assumptions, not only for the happy flow.

Design the timeline for the broken assumptions, not only the happy flow.

BA Takeaway

Test every SDD timeline against all five break scenarios, and ask which parties are open and which calendar applies.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Creditor PSP calendar
→ TARGET calendar
→ Debtor PSP calendar

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this timeline holds when a calendar breaks?"

Have you built a timeline that only worked on a perfect day?
takeaway: Design the timeline for the broken assumptions, not only the happy flow.

title: A EUR 900 direct debit failed for insufficient funds. The scheduler retried it in the wrong order.
explain:
A EUR 900 direct debit fails because the account cannot fund it.
The scheduler retries in first-in-first-out order and fails again.
The salary credit lands two days later, and the D+5 window is almost gone.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 900 debit fails for insufficient funds
→ Scheduler retries in FIFO order
→ Salary credit lands on a later date
→ D+5 window nearly closed

The requirement said:
"Retries should run in first-in-first-out order."

Why?

When a direct debit fails for insufficient funds, retries are confined to the D+5 window of inter-PSP business days, and D+5 is a window, not a penalty or a fine. A scheduler that retries in first-in-first-out order can keep failing, because retry logic is also seasonal: salary credits land on specific dates, and salary accounts hold a balance on those dates. The better requirement checks the balance daily and collects when the account can fund the debit, rather than assuming the scheduler is the optimum solution. Who owns a retry failure, the BA, the developer or the product owner, is a stakeholder agreement, not a technical fact.

D+5 is a window, not a penalty. Collect when the balance can fund it.

BA Takeaway

Check the balance daily inside the D+5 window, collect when the account can fund the debit, and agree who owns a retry failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ D+5 retry window
→ Daily balance check
→ Retry ownership

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this retry was timed to the balance, not to the queue?"

Have you retried a debit on a schedule that ignored payday?
takeaway: D+5 is a window, not a penalty. Collect when the balance can fund it.

title: A EUR 4,000 collection was presented on D-1. The team thought the window had closed at D-14.
explain:
A EUR 4,000 collection is presented to the inter-PSP space.
The team thinks D-14 was the deadline, so the collection must be late.
D-14 opens the window, D-1 closes it, and the collection is inside it.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 4,000 collection presented
→ Team reads D-14 as the submission deadline
→ Collection assumed late
→ Window actually runs D-14 to D-1

The requirement said:
"D-14 is the deadline for presenting a collection."

Why?

D-14 marks the earliest Inter-PSP Business Day for presenting a collection to the Inter-PSP Space, and it doubles as the pre-notification date, by which the debtor must be told about the collection at least 14 calendar days ahead of the Due Date. Receipt by the debtor PSP through the CSM must fall inside that span, with D-1 as the latest permitted day, and for a 15 October Due Date the window is 1 October to 14 October, while the debtor pre-notification in the example went out on 15 September. Confusing D-14 with a submission deadline misreads the rule, since D-14 opens the window and D-1 closes it.

D-14 opens the window. D-1 closes it.

BA Takeaway

Check receipt against the D-14 to D-1 window, and never read D-14 as a deadline.

Keep these controls separate:

→ D-14 opening
→ D-1 closing
→ Debtor pre-notification

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this collection was received inside the window?"

Have you called a collection late when the window had only just opened?
takeaway: D-14 opens the window. D-1 closes it.

title: A EUR 15,000 payment reached the beneficiary in 10 seconds. Compliance had not finished checking it.
explain:
A EUR 15,000 payment reaches the beneficiary in 10 seconds.
The AML and sanctions checks run longer than the payment window allows.
The team wonders whether instant means the checks can be skipped.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 15,000 instant payment sent
→ Beneficiary credited in 10 seconds
→ Compliance checks still running
→ Team asks if checks can be skipped

The requirement said:
"Instant payments move too fast for compliance."

Why?

A payment reaching the beneficiary in 10 seconds still needs AML, sanctions and fraud controls, because instant means compliance must work at payment speed, not that controls disappear. The difficulty is that screening for AML, sanctions and fraud often runs longer than the instant window allows, yet newer technology is making screens smarter and automated, with same-day handling and, in some cases, real-time checks. Once the check sits inside the journey instead of blocking it, instant payments become instant, intelligent and compliant.

Instant means compliance at payment speed, not no compliance.

BA Takeaway

Build the checks inside the instant journey, with smarter automated screening, instead of bolting them on after it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ AML checks
→ Sanctions screening
→ Fraud controls

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the checks ran at payment speed on this payment?"

Have you treated instant as a reason to skip a check?
takeaway: Instant means compliance at payment speed, not no compliance.

title: Intermediary Agent 2 was optional, so a EUR 80,000 payment was left waiting
explain:
A EUR 80,000 cover payment was sent with Intermediary Agent 2 left out.

The message definition says the field is optional, 0..1.

So the sender left it out, and the beneficiary bank held the payment.

Here's how it happened:

→ pacs.008 cover payment sent without Intermediary Agent 2
→ Beneficiary bank receives the payment but cannot see the expected cover path
→ Payment held for cover information
→ Investigation opened, credit delayed

The requirement said:
"Intermediary Agent 2 is optional, so leave it out."

Why?

Message cardinality answers a design question, not a business question. The beneficiary bank needs the intermediary chain to understand where the cover is coming from, and without it the payment cannot be matched with confidence.

Optional in the message does not mean unnecessary in the flow.

BA Takeaway

The working test is not whether the field is mandatory. It is whether the business scenario needs it, who consumes it, and what happens if it is missing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message definition and cardinality
→ Business scenario need
→ Who consumes the field
→ What breaks if it is missing

The real requirement isn't "Is the field mandatory?"

It's "What evidence proves the receiving bank can process this payment without it?"

Have you seen an optional field left out that stopped a payment?
takeaway: Optional in the message does not mean unnecessary in the flow.

title: A bank was EUR 3 million short at settlement, and the last check caught it
explain:
A bank ended the clearing cycle EUR 3 million short on its settlement account.

Settlement was minutes away.

The final check caught the shortfall before the money moved.

Here's how it happened:

→ Participants must hold enough money on the settlement account
→ The mechanism reviews short participants at intervals
→ A bank drifts short during the cycle
→ Final check runs immediately before settlement
→ Shortfall caught, settlement held until the bank funds its account

The assumption was:
"Periodic checks are enough."

Why?

Positions move between checks. A bank that was funded at the last review can be short by settlement time, so the check that matters most is the one just before settlement.

The last check before settlement is the one that saves the cycle.

BA Takeaway

Risk control needs procedures that keep participants funded, interval reviews, and a final check immediately before settlement. No settlement should complete without that last check.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Funding procedures
→ Interval reviews of short participants
→ Final check before settlement
→ Settlement itself

The real requirement isn't "Did we check the positions today?"

It's "What evidence proves every participant is funded right now, before settlement?"

Have you seen a settlement saved by a last-minute funding check?
takeaway: The last check before settlement is the one that saves the cycle.

title: An indirect participant sent EUR 200,000 it did not have, and the direct participant paid for it
explain:
An indirect participant sent a EUR 200,000 debit through its direct participant.

Its account with the direct participant held only EUR 40,000.

The direct participant carried the risk, because accountability for the indirect participant sits with it.

Here's how it happened:

→ Indirect participant funds an account held with the direct participant
→ Debit instruction arrives for EUR 200,000
→ Direct participant draws the money from that account first
→ Funds are insufficient, so the transaction is rejected
→ For a credit, the direct participant credits the indirect participant account and forwards the transaction

The assumption was:
"The indirect participant manages its own risk."

Why?

It does not. The direct participant is accountable for risk arising from indirect participants, so it must check funds before sending a debit on their behalf and reject when the account is short.

Sponsoring a participant means carrying its risk.

BA Takeaway

When a design adds an indirect participant, name who funds the account, who checks before sending, and who absorbs the loss when the funds are not there.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Indirect participant funding
→ Funds check before the debit
→ Rejection when funds are short
→ Credit forwarding

The real requirement isn't "Can the indirect participant send payments?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds were there before the debit was sent?"

Have you seen a direct participant absorb a loss for an indirect participant?
takeaway: Sponsoring a participant means carrying its risk.

title: A mobile number pointed at the wrong account, and INR 25,000 went to a stranger
explain:
A customer sent INR 25,000 to a family member using a mobile number.

The money left the account instantly.

It arrived in a stranger's account, because the proxy resolved to the wrong person.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer enters a mobile number as the beneficiary
→ System resolves the mobile number to an account
→ Resolution rules differ by scheme, and the wrong rule was applied
→ INR 25,000 credited to the wrong account
→ Recovery depends on the stranger agreeing to return it

The assumption was:
"Proxy resolution is a lookup convenience."

Why?

In a linked payment ecosystem, the beneficiary can be identified by a mobile number, a UPI ID or virtual payment address, or a traditional account number. The system must resolve that identifier to the correct account before the payment is sent, and the resolution rules differ by scheme. Getting the proxy resolution wrong sends the money to the wrong person.

Resolution is a payment control, not a lookup.

BA Takeaway

Treat proxy resolution as a control: resolve before sending, confirm the resolved name to the sender, and log the rule that was applied. A wrong resolution is a wrong payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The identifier entered
→ The resolution rule applied
→ The account resolved
→ The name confirmed to the sender before sending

The real requirement isn't "Did the proxy resolve?"

It's "What evidence proves it resolved to the right person?"

Have you seen money go to the wrong person because a proxy resolved wrong?
takeaway: Resolution is a payment control, not a lookup.

title: A customer confirmed a EUR 8,000 transfer, then found the real cost was EUR 8,400
explain:
A customer sent EUR 8,000 across borders.

The screen showed the amount and a confirm button.

After confirming, the customer found the total cost was EUR 8,400, and the delivery date was three days later than expected.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer enters EUR 8,000 to send
→ Screen shows the amount, hides the fee breakdown
→ Exchange rate shown, but not the rate actually applied
→ No expected delivery status shown
→ Customer confirms, then learns the real cost and the real date

The assumption was:
"Transparency can be added as a footnote."

Why?

A customer sending money across borders needs to see the total cost, the applied exchange rate, the fee breakdown, and the expected delivery status before confirming. If any of those are hidden or unclear, the customer cannot judge whether the payment is good value or when it will arrive.

A hidden cost is a broken promise.

BA Takeaway

Transparency is a product requirement, not a nice-to-have, and it has to be designed into the journey, not added as a footnote. Show total cost, applied rate, fee breakdown and delivery status before the confirm button.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Total cost
→ Applied exchange rate
→ Fee breakdown
→ Expected delivery status
→ The confirm button, after all four

The real requirement isn't "Did the customer confirm?"

It's "What evidence proves the customer saw the full cost before confirming?"

Have you seen a customer confirm a payment without seeing its real cost?
takeaway: A hidden cost is a broken promise.

title: A EUR 5,000 payment had to clear in 10 seconds, and the sanctions check needed 40
explain:
A customer sent a EUR 5,000 instant payment.

It had to complete in 10 seconds.

The sanctions check needed 40 seconds, and the team was asked to skip it to meet the speed promise.

Here's how it happened:

→ EUR 5,000 instant payment sent
→ Rail allows 10 seconds to complete
→ Sanctions, anti-money laundering and fraud checks still required
→ Checks take longer than the rail allows
→ Pressure to bypass the checks to meet the speed promise

The assumption was:
"Speed and controls can trade off against each other."

Why?

An instant payment that completes in 10 seconds still needs sanctions, anti-money laundering and fraud checks. The controls must be fast and automated, with a clear escalation path and a full audit trail when a payment is held. The speed target and the control standard have to hold at the same time.

A 10-second payment still needs its controls.

BA Takeaway

Design the controls to fit the rail: fast, automated, with escalation and a full audit trail when a payment is held. Never let a design imply that controls are bypassed to meet the speed promise.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The 10-second speed target
→ Sanctions, AML and fraud checks
→ The escalation path when a payment is held
→ The audit trail, complete

The real requirement isn't "Did the payment complete in 10 seconds?"

It's "What evidence proves the controls ran and the audit trail is complete?"

Have you seen speed pressure used to justify skipping a control?
takeaway: A 10-second payment still needs its controls.

title: A fraudster moved EUR 9,000 out of an account in 20 seconds, before the customer noticed
explain:
A fraudster gained access to a customer's account.

In 20 seconds, EUR 9,000 had left it through instant payments.

The customer noticed the next morning, long after the money was gone.

Here's how it happened:

→ Fraudster gains access to the account
→ Instant payments settle in seconds
→ EUR 9,000 moves out before the customer notices
→ No intervention point stops the flow
→ Post-transaction monitoring finds it the next day, too late

The assumption was:
"One fraud control is enough."

Why?

Instant payments settle in seconds, which is what customers want and what fraudsters want too. An authorised push payment scam can also persuade the customer to send the money themselves. No single control can cover a journey that completes in seconds, so the controls must work together.

Seconds to settle means seconds to steal.

BA Takeaway

Layer the controls: risk signals, velocity checks, confirmation of payee, intervention points, and post-transaction monitoring together. Each one covers a gap the others cannot.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Risk signals
→ Velocity checks
→ Confirmation of payee
→ Intervention points
→ Post-transaction monitoring

The real requirement isn't "Do we have a fraud control?"

It's "What evidence proves the controls together cover a journey that completes in seconds?"

Have you seen a fraud move faster than the controls built to stop it?
takeaway: Seconds to settle means seconds to steal.

title: One pacs.008 for EUR 5 million went to the wrong system, because the route code was never read
explain:
A pacs.008 for EUR 5 million was sent.

It arrived in the wrong settlement system.

The message was perfect. The route code on it was never read.

Here's how it happened:

→ pacs.008 for EUR 5 million prepared
→ BAH BizSvc code declares the route, not the message
→ Payment meant for T2, central bank money settlement via ESMIG to the ECB
→ BizSvc read as a CBPR+ route, sent cross-border through SWIFT FINplus
→ Payment lands in the wrong system, settlement, timing, cost and risk all wrong

The assumption was:
"The message decides the route."

Why?

The same pacs.008 resolves to a different route according to its destination, and the BAH BizSvc code, not the message, declares that route. A T2 payment travels through ESMIG to the ECB, identified by a BizSvc such as trgt.002.001.01, while a CBPR+ payment travels cross-border through SWIFT FINplus, identified by a BizSvc such as swift.cbprplus.02. Because the route sets settlement, timing, cost and risk, a payment routed wrongly can face delay, rejection or incorrect settlement.

The pacs.008 is the instruction. The BAH plus BizSvc is the route.

BA Takeaway

When a pacs.008 is built, check the BAH BizSvc before sending. The message says what to pay. The BizSvc says where it settles.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The pacs.008 instruction
→ The BAH BizSvc route code
→ T2 settlement, central bank money
→ CBPR+ settlement, cross-border

The real requirement isn't "Is the pacs.008 correct?"

It's "What evidence proves the BizSvc matches the intended settlement system?"

Have you seen a payment routed wrong because the BizSvc was never checked?
takeaway: The pacs.008 is the instruction. The BAH plus BizSvc is the route.

title: We hold each other's accounts. Do we still need an intermediary?
explain:
The ordering bank and the beneficiary bank already hold accounts with each other.
A EUR 90,000 international payment needs to move between them.
The operations team still routes it through an intermediary, paying the fee and adding a day, out of habit.

Here's how that happens:

→ Ordering bank and beneficiary bank hold accounts with each other
→ Payment routed through an intermediary anyway
→ Extra fee charged, extra day added

The assumption was:
"An intermediary is always needed for a cross-border payment."

A direct relationship can carry the payment without an intermediary, which is faster and cheaper, but an intermediary may still be used for a currency, a corridor, or a compliance reason. The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved.

Direct is faster and cheaper, but the corridor decides.

BA Takeaway

Test the direct route first. If the accounts exist, the payment can travel directly, and an intermediary is justified only by a currency, corridor or compliance reason that is named, not assumed.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Direct route, faster and cheaper
→ Intermediary for currency needs
→ Intermediary for corridor needs
→ Intermediary for compliance reasons

The real requirement isn't "Do we use an intermediary?"

It's "What evidence proves the intermediary is needed for this corridor?"

Have you ever paid an intermediary fee on a payment that could have gone direct?
takeaway: The choice is a design decision, not a rule, and it depends on the corridor and the banks involved.
